title: White v. Benkowski
summary: Actual inconvenience supported modest compensatory damages for deliberate water interruptions, but malice alone did not support punitive damages on the contract claim presented.
notes: Court: Supreme Court of Wisconsin (1967). The contractual payment and termination details and the two damages rulings were checked against the page image at printed p. 31.

sections.Parties: Virgil and Gwynneth White sued their neighbors Paul and Ruth Benkowski, who supplied water from a well on the Benkowskis’ property.
sections.Material Facts:
The Whites bought a house connected to the neighboring well and entered a written water-supply agreement. It was to run for ten years unless municipal service became available, the well became inadequate, or the Whites obtained their own well. The Whites undertook regular payments and a share of repairs and maintenance.

After relations deteriorated, the Benkowskis interrupted service on nine occasions, generally for less than an hour. They offered explanations involving sediment and excessive use; the jury found that the interruptions were malicious and intended to harass. Mrs. White described resulting inconvenience. The small economic value of the interrupted water did not exhaust that actual injury.
sections.Procedural History: The jury awarded $10 in compensatory damages and $2,000 in punitive damages. The trial court reduced compensation to $1 and eliminated punitive damages. The Supreme Court of Wisconsin reinstated the $10 award while affirming the rejection of punitive damages.
sections.Issue: Did the evidence establish actual loss beyond nominal damages? Could an intentional and malicious breach support punitive damages where no independent tort was pleaded or proved?
sections.Holding: The evidence of inconvenience supported the jury’s small actual-damages award. Punitive damages were unavailable on the contract claim before the court.
sections.Reasoning:
The trial court’s calculation based solely on the contract price of the missing water overlooked inconvenience proved at trial. The jury did not need mathematical precision to award a reasonable amount for actual injury. Its $10 verdict was compensatory, despite being small; it was not merely a symbolic recognition of breach.

The court then separated compensation from punishment. It found no basis for departing from the rule against punitive awards for a breach of contract in the circumstances presented. A contractual relationship can coexist with an independent tort, but no such tort was pleaded or proved here. The jury’s finding of malice therefore did not by itself transform the remedy. The later editorial discussion identifies distinct contexts in which tort claims and punitive relief have been considered; it should not be collapsed into this case’s holding.

priorVersions.summary: Proven inconvenience supported small compensatory damages; malice alone did not authorize punitive damages for this contract breach.
priorVersions.notes: Court: Supreme Court of Wisconsin (1967). The contractual payment and termination details and the two damages rulings were checked against the page image at printed p. 31.

sections.Parties: The Whites received water from their neighbors, the Benkowskis, under a written supply agreement.
sections.Material Facts: The Whites agreed to pay $3 per month and half of future repair or maintenance costs. The contemplated ten-year supply could end under specified conditions, including municipal supply, an inadequate well, or the Whites’ own well. After relations deteriorated, the Benkowskis cut off water on nine occasions. The jury found malicious harassment. The interruptions caused bathroom inconvenience and required trips elsewhere to bathe the children.
sections.Procedural History: The jury awarded $10 compensatory damages and $2,000 punitive damages. The trial court reduced compensation to $1 and eliminated punitive damages. The Wisconsin Supreme Court restored the $10 award while leaving the rejection of punitive damages in place.
sections.Issue: Did inconvenience count as actual contract damage, and could the malicious manner of breach alone support punitive damages?
sections.Holding: The inconvenience justified the jury’s $10 compensatory award. Punitive damages were unavailable for the contract cause of action presented.
sections.Reasoning: Actual loss can include inconvenience even without a precisely proved pecuniary amount. A nominal award instead recognizes a wrong for which actual damage has not been proved. The opinion distinguishes compensation from punishment and does not treat an intentional or malicious breach as automatically an independent tort. The subsequent notes discuss separate tort theories and disputes over their boundaries; those examples do not change this decision’s disposition.

learning.why: The case requires two separate classifications: actual versus nominal compensation, and compensation versus punishment.

topics.nominal-damages: A small award can compensate proved injury rather than merely acknowledge a right.
topics.punitive-damages: Malicious breach alone did not establish a punitive remedy in this case.
topics.remedies: The legal theory and nature of the loss control different parts of the analysis.
